name: Sua
confidence_why: Segerer 2024, the only description of Sua prosody, tentatively assumes no lexical tone and notes only that long vowels sound more intense, possibly an artefact of elicitation, so no stress placement or type is on record; Wilson 2007 has no prosody section for Sua and Segerer's 2017 wordlist marks neither stress nor tone.

catalog_quote: Prosody When pronounced in isolation, lexical items show quite clear melodies, but these melodies tend to vary from one | utterance to another. new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress-placement rule is given. The only prosodic statement is that pitch melodies on isolated words are clear but unstable across utterances, so no lexical tone is assumed 'at this stage of description'; the one intensity observation (long vowels louder) is explicitly discounted as a possible elicitation artefact. The chapter never uses the word 'stress' or 'accent' (Google page-level index). Word stress is therefore undescribed for Sua; the source is agnostic, not a 'no stress' claim.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author flags the whole description as very tentative (few lexical data, two dialects, unpublished Doneux/Wilson notes plus 1998 Bissau recordings).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical items pronounced in isolation (elicitation); nothing on phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement concerns Sua as recorded by Segerer (Bissau 1998 recordings plus Doneux and Wilson notes); Segerer notes at least two dialectal variants (Wilson 1961c: 'Lower' vs 'Upper' Sua) without saying which the prosody remark covers. Glottolog mans1259 has no dialect-level languoids. Not to be confused with Sua (Bila) of DR Congo.
